blocks.text: Who we are
Matt Anderson started Mere Orthodoxy in 2005. Today 1,531 Members pay for it. We publish essays most weekdays along with a print journal, a free library, three podcasts and four ebooks.

The name comes from two books. C.S. Lewis wrote Mere Christianity and G.K. Chesterton wrote Orthodoxy. Both men believed Christians share a core of the faith across their traditions and that it holds up under scrutiny. We take the Nicene Creed as the summary of that shared faith.
Tagline
Mission
Forming Christians in the Church to participate in culture for the common good.
We do that by drawing on the whole Christian tradition and bringing it to the questions people are asking now.
Two convictions
The first is Protestant catholicity. We're Protestants of the Reformation who still claim the whole church's inheritance as our own.
The second is solidarity conservatism. We want to keep what has made Western life good. We also believe people live in membership with one another as bearers of God's image.
The Mere Orthodoxy Code

items.label: Rooted Orthodoxy in a Fractured World

body.text: We hold to Nicaea and to what Scripture teaches about sex and gender. We take the world as God made it.

items.label: Christian Love in an Angry World

body.text: We defend Christian beliefs in Christian ways. That means choosing hope over fear and refusing power plays.

items.label: Patient Reflection in a Reactive World

body.text: We take the time to think before we write. The questions that matter most will still be there next week.

items.label: Irenic Hearts in a Partisan World

body.text: We try to say what's good and true in words worth reading. We don't sort people into teams or defer to credentials.

items.label: Redemptive Media in a Distracted World

body.text: We think reason and persuasion are real goods. Media can still shape how people imagine the world.

blocks.text: We sit near the top on the public square side. Our essays on politics, technology and the family argue from theology. First Things is our nearest neighbor there. It's mostly Catholic and more combative, and readers name it when they say what they're glad we're not. Plough and Comment write about the public square too but lean less on theology. Sola Media and Truth Unites are as theological as we are but write mostly about the Church. Christianity Today, WORLD and The Gospel Coalition cover the church with news and opinion.
Readers also say we don't map onto either side of American politics. They call us "irenic" and say we're "one of the few intelligent voices."

Anyone can read us. The readers who pay lead churches: 40% of Members are pastors, elders or deacons. Our readers' first stop is still The Gospel Coalition. Half of our Subscribers and 57% of our Members read it.

blocks.text: Voice
We write like an educated pastor at the kitchen table. He's read deeply and thought hard. He's talking to you with the coffee on and the kids in the next room. He doesn't talk down to you.

We're tender with people and firm with ideas. We can be sharp about a movement or an ideology and still be gentle with the people caught up in it. We give the other side its best case and grant what's true in it before we say what it misses.
We start with something concrete. A child up at 2 a.m. looking for her doll teaches more about dependence than a statistic does. Then we make the claim the detail supports.
We explain how we got here. The history of a problem is part of the problem. We name what's broken without despairing over it. Our humor is dry (and never sarcastic).
We write from settled convictions. You won't see us open with "In light of recent events."
Our readers told us in the 2025 survey that we use too many $5 words. When we write for new readers, the plain word wins.
House rules
These cover every word written as Mere Orthodoxy or as a member of our staff. Headlines and buttons count.

body.text: Use contractions. Keep it short. When in doubt, cut it in half. Give real names, dates and numbers.
In our own copy a comma, a colon, parentheses or a new sentence usually reads better. An essay can keep one where nothing else works. Quotations keep theirs.
Don't join two sentences with a comma. Don't bolt a clause on with ", and" or ", but." Don't hang a phrase off the end of a sentence either.

items.text: The reading is free, the tools are paid.
The reading is free. The tools are paid.

body.text: Not in headings, emphasis or book titles. When something needs emphasis, it gets the terracotta highlight or a heavier weight.
Titles and quotations keep the spelling they were printed with.
Words like leading, seminal and profound don't tell the reader anything. State the fact or leave it out.
If a page wouldn't lose anything without a sentence, the sentence goes. Reassurances, disclaimers and taglines tucked under titles usually go first.
Never frame anything as "good news." In member email, things get fixed. They never get deployed or shipped.
When copy is about the translations in The Faith Received, say that many of them were made with AI. A passing mention of the library doesn't need the note.

blocks.text: Words we don't use

body.text: your truth, safe space, we're all on a journey
blessed, God is doing a new thing (unless you say what thing)
curate, optimize, leverage, empower, unlock, elevate
delve, tapestry, testament to, seamless, game-changing
friend, y'all, we're all just figuring this out

blocks.text: Also watch for the habits that make copy sound machine-made. Punchy one-line paragraphs give it away. So do lines that announce their own importance and the "It's not X, it's Y" move.
By format

body.text: Essays run 1,500 to 4,000 words and may keep long, layered sentences. Most open on a concrete scene or a real question.
There's no formula. Plain and literary both work. "Blueprint for Renewal" and "In Praise of Being Inconvenient" are both ours. Skip listicles and search bait like "5 Ways to Fix the American Church."
Open with something from ordinary life and make one turn. Close with an invitation. Don't beg and don't hype.
Pair one vivid image with one claim and the link. Don't explain the connection.
Tell the problem as a piece of history. Then say what we're doing about it and leave out the superlatives.
Leave off source footers, taglines under titles and template title slides. The cover is our logo and the title in the highlight.

blocks.text: Copywriting
These rules come from what we've already published. We read the site's templates, our latest 100 essays and the Weekly Digest. Where the site is inconsistent, the more common form wins.

blocks.text: Form

body.text: Title case. In our latest 100 essays, 99 use it. Keep small words lowercase ("to be," "is in") and capitalize the word after a colon. A median headline runs seven words. About three in ten take the form "Evocative phrase: Plain subject."
Every essay gets one. Make it a full sentence from the essay, ending with a period. Most run about 25 words.
Sentence case: "Save your seat," "Start reading," "Subscribe free." Become a Member is the one exception. The Digest's buttons follow the same rule.
Roman, with no italics. In running copy they need nothing else. In a headline or dek, put them in single quotes: 'That Hideous Strength.'
"By" and the name on cards. Join two writers with "and."
"An Interview with" and the name.
November 12, 2026. Write days of the week out: "every Thursday."
Spell out a number that starts a sentence: "Eleven essays." Use numerals elsewhere, with commas from 1,000.
"$100/yr" on a pricing card. "$100 a year" in a sentence.
Write C.S. Lewis with no space between the initials. Use curly apostrophes and quotation marks.

blocks.text: What the site needs to fix

The membership pages and the gift page say "Audio versions of every article." Several buttons are in title case ("Get The Journal," "Start Now," "Renew Membership"). Four Faith Received pages say "Become a member." The about page says "the print Journal" and calls our shows "postcasts." The byline sits in italics on every essay. Each Digest subject line has an em dash.
The editorial style guide now matches. Headlines take title case and titles are set roman.
Logo
The mark is a city of spires inside a circle. The full lockup sets it beside the wordmark and Est. MMV, which is 2005 in Roman numerals.

The icon on avatars, favicons and podcast badges

blocks.text: Give the lockup room. The clear space around it should be at least half the icon's width. Below 140 pixels wide on screen or 1.25 inches in print, switch to the icon.
The white logo never sits on the bright orange because the contrast is too weak. Put it on the darker terracotta instead. On a photograph, set the white logo over a calm, dark patch of the image.
Don't recolor, stretch, outline or shadow the mark. Don't reset the wordmark in another typeface either.

blocks.text: Typography
We use two typefaces and never set either one in italics.

IM Fell Great Primer is our display face. It's for title pages, chapter titles, the Journal masthead and the titles of works. Keep it off anything a reader works with: lists, labels, buttons and charts. Keep it off numbers too. Figures, prices, dates and numerals all set in Source Serif. IM Fell has one weight, so never bold it.

blocks.sample: Instinct after instinct was answered by doctrine after doctrine.
blocks.text: Source Serif Pro is our working face. It sets the body text, buttons, labels, navigation, captions and every number.
Sizes

There's no sans serif anywhere. Monospace is only for code. Minion Pro was the body face in the first guide and it's gone from the web. The redesigned Journal sets in IM Fell and Source Serif 4. The Daily Liturgy uses Source Serif 4 alone.
The page

body.text: A terracotta band sits behind the key words of a headline and sweeps in once from the left as the page loads. We use it where other publications would use italics.
A pilcrow between two hairlines marks a break between sections. A fleuron closes a long list.
The first letter of an opening paragraph gets IM Fell and terracotta. It sits in the line instead of floating beside it.
We number with Roman numerals when the order means something, as with the Journal's sections. They set in Source Serif, never IM Fell. Ordinary lists don't get them.
Every rule on screen is one pixel in the rule color. Frames in print and video use a heavier line with a weight of 3.
Tan sections and the navigation carry a faint paper texture. Nothing else does.
Contributors appear in circles. When there's no photo, the circle shows their initial in Source Serif.
Each page opens on a dark hero and usually has one more dark band lower down. A soft terracotta glow sits in one corner.

blocks.text: The button
There's one button on the site. It rests hollow inside a thin ink outline with 3px corners. Its label is in sentence case. When you hover, terracotta sweeps across it from the left.
Each page gets one solid button for its main ask. On a dark band the outline turns white.
What we leave out

We don't use floating cards with shadows or pill-shaped buttons. Nothing scrolls inside its own box on the page, though sidebars and drawers are fine. We skip decorative gradients, emoji and badges. Motion stays under a third of a second and respects a reader's reduced-motion setting.
Photography
We want our photos to look like a lifestyle shoot on Fujifilm film. Shoot in real light and put the Journal in someone's hands.

items.alt: Journal on a table in soft light
items.caption: Airy

blocks.text: Let the light decide. A frame shot in hard shade can go dark with true blacks. A frame in sun or through glass stays bright with clean whites. Never darken it.

Film character comes from color. Look for true oranges and skin, greens leaning toward olive, highlights that roll off softly and a fine grain. Keep it restrained. That means no heavy vignettes, muddy midtones, orange-and-teal grading or HDR.
The Journal's cover has to read as a saturated orange. If it looks cocoa or dusty pink, the grade is wrong.
Our subjects are books, the Journal, coffee and linen. The hands and tables are real. We don't present AI renders as photographs. Our mockups of an issue we haven't printed stay internal.

blocks.text: Sub-brands
The Daily Liturgy has its own look. The Faith Received uses the magazine's look with a few rules of its own. Christians Reading Classics and the forums are in chapters IV and VIII.
The Daily Liturgy
Coram Deo Church makes The Daily Liturgy in partnership with Mere Orthodoxy. It wears copper on a gray ground and never the magazine's terracotta or tan.

Everything sets in Source Serif 4. The script wordmark is its only display element, so IM Fell never appears. Its signature is the copper double rule from the podcast cover. The rule is inset from the edge and has a scalloped ornament in each corner.
Section labels are uppercase and letterspaced. Always show the address as dailyliturgy.com.
The Faith Received
The library uses the magazine's colors and its one button. Its tools stay compact. Body text runs 15 to 16px and the headers are slim.
IM Fell appears only on chapter titles, shelf names and period pieces like a title page. The library speaks for the texts. Its descriptions never say "we" or explain where Mere Orthodoxy stands.
Brand pieces
Quote cards

One template makes quote cards in five sizes: link, portrait, square, story and X. Each brand gets its own version. Ours sets the quote in Source Serif on the page color with a short terracotta rule above it. The speaker goes in small terracotta capitals with the source under them. The lockup sits at the foot. The Faith Received's cards use cream and the library's name instead of the logo.

Channels
How readers become Members

body.text: An essay reaches them through a friend, social media, search or The Faith Received.
They sign up for the Weekly Digest, download an ebook, register for a forum or open a free library account.
The Digest, the podcasts and The Daily Liturgy do that work over months and years.
Usually the Journal, Mere Fidelity or a direct ask tied to a piece they loved tips them over.
A new issue in the mailbox each season keeps them. So do the Mailbag, the Discord and the forum replays.
